title: Determine the Whole Given the Part and Percent
objective: I can determine the whole when I know a part and the percent that part represents.
model: double number line (known part under its percent, step to 10% or 1%, count up to 100%) and the equation Whole = Part ÷ Percent

widgets.component: '15 is 30% of what number?': find 1% (part ÷ percent), then × 100
widgets.root: A unit-rate route to the whole that is mathematically equivalent to the lesson's 10%-step and Part ÷ Percent methods; all eight wholes verified (50, 30, 60, 70, 30, 50, 60, 140).

widgets.component: '25% of a number is 18. Find the whole.' with a tape of N equal chunks
widgets.root: The figure's header and caption print '1 chunk (25%) = 18' and '4 × 18 = 72', i.e. the whole. Only percents that divide 100 evenly (25, 20, 50, 10) appear, so the chunk count is never a decision. Static SVG; nothing to manipulate.
widgets.replacement: Replace with a double number line: percent row 0-100 below, amount row above, the known part placed at its percent, a blank at 100%. The student picks the step (10% or 5%), shades that many steps from 0 to the known part, and types the amount of one step and then the whole; use 60%, 15%, 45% so the step is not simply the given part. No caption of the product.

widgets.where: Practice Tab 3 (8: Whole = Part ÷ Percent as decimal)
widgets.root: The formula the lesson derives, in its own order; all wholes verified.

widgets.where: Practice Tab 4 (8 stories: cheese sticks, fruit, veggie sticks, test problems, coupon, free throws, novel pages, auditorium seats)
widgets.component: typed whole from a part and a percent
12 is 25%, 30 is 50%, which equation, 45 is 90%, 7 is 10%, pizza 20%, 21 is 75%, 1% = 3.5, 1 bar = 3 hours, 16 is 32%
widgets.root: On objective; keys correct; item 3 asks for the equation rather than a number.
Question, method and answer matched; tiles generated from the numbers, so no label can disagree.

widgets.component: whole from a part with percents above 100 and below 1
widgets.root: Part ÷ Percent with decimal percents; the answers are right (80, 150, 800, 1,800, 120, 6,000, 300, 2,000) and the wrong-path feedback separates dividing by the wrong number.

widgets.component: sold types make 60% = 120 puzzles, total 200, then a remaining type
widgets.root: Combines percents then finds the whole; all eight verified (200, 80, 200, 700, 300, 600, 140, 200).

widgets.where: Challenge Tab 3 (8 reverse discounts and take-home pay, three-choice mc)
widgets.component: after 20% off, $48; after 15% tax, $850; 30% off, $84; tank loses 40%; why adding 20% to a sale price does not restore it
widgets.root: Correct and a good extension (the whole is 100% − discount), but the right choice always shows its working ('$60 ($48 is 80% ... ÷ 0.80)') while distractors are bare numbers.
widgets.replacement: Same-shape choices (a dollar amount) with the working in the feedback; add a typed 'what percent of the original is the sale price?' field before the choice (80%, 85%, 70%, 75%, 60%, 35%, 12%).

widgets.component: find the total from one known count and its percent, then another category
widgets.root: Whole then part; tables are consistent (100% sums) and every total verified (300, 320, 180, 300, 160, 400).

widgets.component: '40% liked dogs, 35% cats, 25% birds. 150 students liked dogs and birds combined (65%). Total survey size?' key 230.77
widgets.root: 150 ÷ 0.65 is 230.77, so the item's key is a fractional number of students; no survey has 230.77 respondents. The context makes the problem impossible and teaches that a non-integer headcount is acceptable.
widgets.replacement: Use 130 students (65% of 200) in the stem; key 200; options 200, 195, 130 (the part), 845 (130 × 6.5).
